title: What Claude Code's multi-agent code review costs and finds
summary: On Sonnet 5.5, /code-review max matched 23 of 27 serious answer-key issues in 56 min for $21 a finished review; one agent matched 21 for $0.11.
body_markdown:
## TL;DR


**Claude Code’s multi-agent` /code-review max` caught 23 of 27 serious bugs on hard pull requests, against 21 for a single agent, but cost about $21 a review instead of 11 cents and took 56 minutes instead of 40 seconds.**


- **The trade-off.** Two more bugs is close to this benchmark’s noise, and the multi-agent review also made twice as many claims you have to read. Still, one serious bug in production can cost far more than $21, so it comes down to what a missed bug costs your team.
- **How I measured it.** 20 hard pull requests from a public benchmark, with Sonnet 5.5 doing the work in both settings to keep the bill manageable.
- **What I’d do.** Start with` /code-review high` on Opus 5.5: across all 50 benchmark PRs it caught 51 of 66 serious bugs for about 36 cents each. If you run` max` , read its transcript to see which subagents actually ran, because some of mine skipped verification to stay under budget.


Anthropic’s Claude Code team has[written down how it reviews code](https://claude.dev/blog/solving-code-review-at-anthropic/) : several agents look for bugs at once, “then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it’s real.” Anthropic’s Deputy CISO, Jason Clinton,[calls narrow review agents](https://claude.com/resources/articles/how-anthropic-secures-its-ai-native-software-development-lifecycle) “much more effective than one mega-prompt or super security agent.” Those posts are about Anthropic’s managed service and its internal process, and neither gives a count of the bugs the agents find or miss per pull request, how much else they say, how long a review takes or what it costs. The local` /code-review` command that ships with Claude Code, which in the team’s words “runs a lighter version locally”, has the same shape at its` max` setting and is the one anyone can run, so I measured it.


I ran Claude Code’s local` /code-review` command, not Anthropic’s managed Code Review service1 , with one agent and with its multi-agent fan-out, scored both on 20 pull requests from a public benchmark5 , and put them against Quickchat Review, the reviewer I built4 . The benchmark’s own score put the three leading reviews within 0.8 points of each other, so I also had two AI judges compare the reviews head to head10 .


**With its agents on Sonnet 5.5, the fan-out does catch bugs. It does not catch all of them, it takes most of an hour, it adds twice as many claims that the answer key does not list, and it cost $20.95 per finished review.**8 Quickchat Review works on the same idea, many narrow AI reviewers and a check before anything is posted. On Opus 5.5 the judges’ ratings do not separate it from the fan-out, and it got there for $4.61 and 8.2 minutes per pull request, under a quarter of the fan-out’s recorded price per finished review and about a seventh of its wall-clock time under our concurrency and rate limits.


## What I measured


**The product.** Claude Code 2.1.3031 and its local[/code-review command](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-local) , a skill bundled with the CLI that works on any plan and bills to your usage or API key; Anthropic’s managed[Code Review service](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review) is a separate product I did not test.


**How it ran.** Headless, in a locked-down Docker sandbox with no GitHub token and no GitHub writes2 :


```text
claude   -p   '/code-review high <base>...<head>'   --output-format   json
```


In Claude Code’s own transcripts,` high` and` max` select two different review recipes, and the documentation describes neither3 . At` high` it starts one agent:` high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings` . At` max` it fans out:` max effort → 5+5 angles × 8 candidates → 1-vote verify → sweep → ≤15 findings` , about ten finder agents, a verifier agent per candidate, then a sweep. To make` max` affordable on twenty PRs I forced every subagent onto Sonnet 5.5, capped each review at $30 and gave it 90 minutes4 ; none of that is a shipped default, and neither are the rest of my settings2 . The two recipes differ in more than their number of agents, so this compares the two settings Claude Code ships, not parallelism alone3 .


*The three review shapes compared in this post, each as its tool intends it.*


**The benchmark.** Martian’s[Code Review Bench](https://github.com/withmartian/code-review-benchmark) : 20 of its 50 PRs from Sentry, Grafana, Cal.com, Discourse and Keycloak, scored by Martian’s own pipeline with one LLM judge, GPT-6.1 Sol, for every reviewer7 . Its pipeline splits each review into claims and matches them against the key; a claim that matches nothing is an unmatched claim7 . Twenty and not fifty because the full set of` max` reviews would have cost about $1,000 and run for about 16 hours5 . The 20 are the PRs where Quickchat Review on two other models had done worst, a selection expected to favour every other reviewer; Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.5 and Quickchat Review on Sonnet 5.5 also ran on all 505 .


**Costs and times.** Claude Code’s dollar figures are the estimates it records for each session, apart from one recount labelled where it appears, and Quickchat Review’s are computed from token usage, both at list prices; every time is wall-clock with several reviews running at once89 .` max` has three cost figures, each labelled where it appears: $20.95 per finished review, $19.90 over all 20 PRs in the charts, and about $440 actually spent8 .


## The fan-out matched two more serious issues than one agent


Both runs reviewed the same 20 PRs with Sonnet 5.5 doing the work4 . The fan-out matched two more of the 27 serious answer-key issues and the same number of issues overall; two issues is about the scoring noise on this benchmark, so I cannot say whether that difference would repeat7 . Match counts are totals over the 20 PRs and the other rows are means; the` max` column’s time and cost rest on its 19 finished reviews, and its match and claim counts cover all 20, with the timed-out review counted as zero and five reviews scored from reports recovered from their transcripts9 .


Metric` /code-review high` (1 agent)` /code-review max` (16.5 agents a review)


Serious answer-key issues matched, 20 PRs together (27 in the key) 21 23


All answer-key issues matched, 20 PRs together (65 in the key) 47 47


Unmatched claims, mean per PR 11.9 23.9


Wall-clock time, mean per finished review 40 s 56 min


Recorded cost, mean per finished review $0.11 (20 of 20 finished) $20.95 (19 of 20 finished)


The fan-out still missed 4 of the 27 serious issues. It produced twice as many unmatched claims, and its recorded subtotal was 188 times one agent’s, $398.03 against $2.128 .


*On the same 20 hard PRs with Sonnet 5.5, Claude Code` max` matched 2 more serious answer-key issues than` high` and the same number overall. The chart’s $19.90 a review spreads the recorded subtotal over all 20 PRs; per finished review it is $20.95.*


## What happens inside a max review


**The unforced configuration, on one small PR.** On browser-use #857, a 97-line change with five defects in our answer key6 ,` /code-review high` on Opus 5.5 found all five in 70 seconds for 32 cents.` max` with Opus 5.5 on every agent4 started 9 finder agents and 14 verifiers, made 608 API calls and had spent **$40.64** , by our recount of those calls8 , when our 30-minute limit stopped it at 31 minutes. It printed nothing, because Claude Code prints the review only when it finishes.


*Cumulative cost of the all-Opus 5.5` max` run on browser-use #857 until the 30-minute limit stopped it with nothing printed, with the` high` run on Opus 5.5 as the dot near the origin.*


**The model running the recipe decides how much of it runs.** Same` max` prompt, same PR, a different model forced onto the review agent and every child: Opus 5.5 launched 9 finders and 14 verifiers, Sonnet 5.5 launched 5 finders and no verifiers, and Haiku 5.5 launched no finders and 5 verifiers6 . The Sonnet run cost $13.31 and took 32 minutes, the Haiku run $0.53 and 13.5 minutes, and both found all five defects. Each is a single run, and the Sonnet and Haiku runs had a $15 budget cap the agents could see, while the Opus run had none6 .


*Opus 5.5 launched nearly all of the` max` recipe and printed nothing before the limit, while Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 each skipped part of it and still found all five defects.*


**Agents cut work when they can see the budget.** Five of the 19 finished` max` reviews launched no verifier at all. The agents can see a running budget line in their context, and four of the five named it as the reason, one in these words: “Per-candidate verifier agents were skipped because of budget.”3 No review reached the $30 cap, so an uncapped` max` might run more verifiers and cost more3 .


**Cost did not track PR size.** Finished reviews cost $15.17 to $26.09 each, with only a weak association with changed lines (r = 0.18)8 .


*Claude Code` max` with Sonnet 5.5 agents spent $15 to $26 on every finished hard PR, close to the $30 cap it could see, while` high` on Sonnet 5.5 stayed between six and sixteen cents.*


**The verifier checks that a bug is real, not that the PR introduced it.** In the all-Opus` max` run on browser-use #857 the verifiers assessed 18 candidate bugs, marked 16 confirmed and 2 plausible, and refuted none; two of the confirmed bugs existed before the PR6 .


**Several reviews exited successfully without a usable report.** Five of the twenty` max` reviews returned a closing note instead of the review, for example: “The last background agents have finished. The report above stands, with no findings to add or remove.” Those five PRs delivered 2 of their 63 findings. One review ran into the 90-minute limit without a report, and 25 of 339 agents died on rate-limit errors from our API key, 23 of them inside 11 reviews that still reported success, so a check of the exit status alone would have missed all of this9 .


## The answer key could not separate the leaders


The answer key did rank the reviews:` max` scored 30.0 on the benchmark’s F2, well below the leaders. It did not separate the leaders: Quickchat Review on Sonnet 5.5 at 43.9, Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.5 at 43.2 and Claude Code` high` on Sonnet 5.5 at 43.1, three very different setups within 0.8 points. Martian’s key holds about 3.7 entries per PR, the reviews made 8 to 26 claims per PR, and the key cannot tell a true claim it lacks from a wrong one7 .


So I added a second instrument: a judge that reads two reviews of the same PR side by side, with the diff, the touched files and the answer key, and says which one a maintainer would rather receive, with a verdict each for recall, precision, finding quality and writing10 . Two judges from different providers, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, rated 298 matchups each with identical prompts10 , and the results are on the Elo scale, over the reviews that exist11 .


## What the judges found


The judges rated the fan-out highest, though not clearly above Quickchat Review on Opus 5.5. The five main configurations on the same 20 PRs:

Match counts are totals over the 20 PRs, unmatched claims are means over all 20, and time and cost are means, for` max` over its 19 finished reviews8 . Rows on the same model compare complete configurations, which differ in more than the harness; Quickchat Review also ran six quality passes on GPT-6 Luna, under 2% of its cost4 .


*The review the answer key scores last, Claude Code` max` with Sonnet 5.5 agents, is the one the judges rate highest.*


The judges credited` max` with findings the answer key does not list: over their 194 recall verdicts on its pairs it won 162, tied 22 and lost 10. It also came last on writing, with 14 wins against 179 losses11 . Against` high` on Opus 5.5 it rates +148 (95% interval +64 to +241), about a 70% expected win rate under the fitted model, at 61 times the recorded cost; that margin comes mostly from the Opus judge, and the GPT judge on its own does not separate the two11 . It rates 38 points above Quickchat Review on Opus 5.5, with a 95% interval from −33 to +135: the interval includes zero, so these data do not say which of the two is better11 .


*Among the five main setups, the judges rate Claude Code` max` with Sonnet 5.5 agents best at finding problems and worst at precision and at writing them up.*


The two judges agreed on precision 76% of the time and on recall 70%, but on the overall winner only 56%, and each judge’s highest-rated configuration ran on its own model family12 . GPT favoured lean reviews and Opus thorough ones, so the overall ranking rests on how much a missed bug weighs against a wasted comment; the recall, precision and writing verdicts are where the two judges mostly agree.


*The two judges named the same overall winner in only 56% of matchups, but agreed far more often on recall, precision and writing.*


## Start with` /code-review high` on Opus 5.5


For an inexpensive first pass, I would start with` /code-review high` on Opus 5.5. It reviewed every one of the 50 benchmark PRs in 42 to 151 seconds for about 36 cents and matched 51 of the 66 serious answer-key issues, so it also missed 155 . On the twenty hard PRs the judges rated it 120 points above the same command on Sonnet 5.5 (1518 against 1398), a gap whose interval only just excludes zero11 , though the Sonnet 5.5 version costs about a third as much. Run it on your branch before you open a PR, which is the use its documentation describes. It gives no severity, no verdict and no clean split between bugs the PR introduced and bugs that were already there, and its prompt asks for at most ten findings unless you pass` --max-findings` , a request rather than an enforced limit3 .


I would not run` max` on every PR. Anthropic’s model-configuration documentation says the` max` effort level[“may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking, so test before adopting it broadly”](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/model-config) , and users have reported long, costly multi-agent review runs on Claude Code’s issue tracker3 . If you do try it headless, cap the budget (the agents can see it and may cut work to fit), set a timeout, keep the transcripts, and check that what came back is a review and not a closing note9 .


## How Quickchat Review compares, and where it differs


Quickchat Review runs a planned set of narrow review passes, each looking for one kind of problem, then a validator meant to check every candidate before anything is posted4 . In cost and time it sits between one Claude Code agent and the fan-out. On Sonnet 5.5 it produced the fewest unmatched claims of the eight configurations I ran, 6.2 per PR against 11.9 for one Claude Code agent and 23.9 for the fan-out on the same model, and the judges ranked it first of all eight reviewers on precision and on writing; it also matched fewer answer-key issues, 37 against 47 for one Claude Code agent. On Opus 5.5 the judges’ ratings do not separate it from` max` , at $4.61 and 8.2 minutes per PR against $20.95 and 56 minutes, though it produced 16.2 unmatched claims per PR there, more than any other configuration in the five-row table except` max`7 . On all 50 PRs its Sonnet 5.5 build matched 49 of 66 serious issues at $1.32 a PR, against 51 of 66 at 36 cents for Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.55 . Both versions give every finding a severity and end with a verdict, which none of the Claude Code runs do.


*Cost per pull request on a log scale against the two judges’ combined Elo for all eight reviewers on the same 20 PRs, with a dashed line joining the best rating at each cost.*


Quickchat AI will open-source Quickchat Review in the coming weeks. How its workflow differs from Claude Code’s, and what is still open:


- **One finding per root cause, with a severity and a verdict.** It posts blockers, questions and nits, and decides approve or request changes, with approval withheld while CI is red.
- **A validator meant to keep old bugs out.** It checks each candidate against the code and drops or flags problems that existed before the PR; on Opus 5.5 it ran on every PR, and on Sonnet 5.5 two of the 20 reviews skipped it9 . Claude Code’s verifier checks whether a claim is true, not whether the PR introduced it6 .
- **Several model families.** The tested builds ran on Claude, GPT, DeepSeek and GLM models; on GLM-5.3 Flash it cost 60 cents a PR on the same twenty8 .
- **The harness must enforce the review stages it plans.** On Sonnet 5.5 Quickchat Review cut its own plan too: on two PRs it ran none of its review passes, wrote “I skipped the lens passes and the validator and reviewed the diff myself,” and approved one of them9 . A step that only a prompt asks for can be skipped, in either tool; the fix is for the harness to launch each planned pass itself, count them and fail the review when one is missing.
- **Not tested here:** follow-up rounds, replies to the author and repository-specific setup15 .


It is not cheaper than Claude Code’s single agent: on the same model it costs 11 to 14 times as much as` high` . On the answer key its F2 on Sonnet 5.5 is 0.8 points above` high` ’s (43.9 against 43.1), a gap these data cannot separate, and on Opus 5.5 it trails (35.0 against 43.2). The judges preferred it over` high` on Opus 5.5 (+110, interval +31 to +196), though as with` max` that margin comes mostly from the Opus judge11 , and on Sonnet 5.5 for precision and writing. Whether that is worth the price depends on what a missed bug and a wasted comment each cost your team.


## Limitations


This is one run per configuration on 20 PRs chosen where Quickchat Review had done worst5 , with costs as each tool records or computes them and times under our concurrency and rate limits89 , Claude Code under our sandbox settings rather than an untouched default2 , LLM judges with no human check that share model families with some of the reviewers12 , and a builder of a competing reviewer, partly tuned on this benchmark’s PRs, running the tests14 . The rest are in note 1515 , and every raw result will be published with the open-source release16 .


## Frequently asked questions


### How much does Claude Code’s /code-review max cost per pull request?


About $21 per finished review in my runs: $20.95 recorded on average over the 19 of 20 benchmark PRs whose review finished, with every subagent forced onto Sonnet 5.5 under a $30 cap, and $15.17 to $26.09 per finished review. Counting the timed-out review and the abandoned attempts that were re-run, the true spend was about $440, or about $22 a PR. The all-Opus 5.5 configuration had spent $40.64 on one 97-line PR when a 30-minute limit stopped it, and one agent at high effort cost $0.11 per PR on Sonnet 5.5 and $0.33 on Opus 5.5, with every review finished.


### How long does a Claude Code /code-review max review take?


56 minutes of wall-clock time on average over the 19 reviews that finished, with three to five reviews running at once on one API key whose rate limits are below Anthropic’s standard tier, and one review was still running at a 90-minute limit. The single-agent high setting took 40 seconds on average on Sonnet 5.5 and 78 seconds on Opus 5.5 on the same 20 PRs, and 42 to 151 seconds on Opus 5.5 across all 50 PRs of the benchmark.


### Does Claude Code’s multi-agent fan-out find more bugs than one agent?


On 20 benchmark PRs with Sonnet 5.5 doing the work, the max fan-out matched 23 of the 27 Critical or High answer-key issues and one agent at high matched 21, and both matched 47 of the 65 issues overall. Two issues is about the scoring noise on this benchmark, and with one run per configuration I cannot say whether that difference would repeat. The fan-out produced twice as many claims that matched nothing in the key, 23.9 per PR against 11.9, at 188 times the recorded cost, $398.03 against $2.12.


### What is the difference between /code-review high and max in Claude Code?


In Claude Code 2.1.303 they select different review recipes, which the documentation does not describe and which depend on the model as well as the effort level. At high, the recipe asks one agent to work through eight review angles in its own context, deduplicate and report at most ten findings, with no verifier stage. At max, it asks the orchestrator to launch about ten finder subagents, then one verifier subagent per candidate, where a single vote that does not refute a finding keeps it, then a sweep, and to report at most fifteen findings; in my runs the model sometimes launched fewer agents than that. The —max-findings option replaces both limits.


### Is the local /code-review command the same as Anthropic’s managed Code Review?


No. The local /code-review command is a skill bundled with the Claude Code CLI that runs in your own session on any plan and bills as usage or to an API key, while Anthropic’s managed Code Review is a GitHub App for Team and Enterprise plans that runs on Anthropic’s infrastructure and adds severity tags. Anthropic’s documentation calls them two separate tools, and this post measured only the local command.


### Which Claude Code review setting is good enough for most pull requests?


For an inexpensive first pass, /code-review high on Opus 5.5: it reviewed all 50 benchmark PRs in 42 to 151 seconds for about 36 cents each and matched 51 of the 66 serious answer-key issues, so it also missed 15. On Sonnet 5.5 it costs about a third as much. It gives no severity and no verdict, its prompt asks for at most ten findings unless you pass —max-findings, and Anthropic’s model-configuration documentation warns that the max effort level may show diminishing returns and is prone to overthinking.


### How does Quickchat Review compare with Claude Code’s /code-review?


Two LLM judges’ ratings do not separate Quickchat Review on Opus 5.5 from the max fan-out with Sonnet 5.5 agents, 1628 against 1666 Elo with a 95% interval on the gap that includes zero, at $4.61 and 8.2 minutes per PR against $20.95 and 56 minutes per finished max review under our rate limits. On Sonnet 5.5 it produced the fewest unmatched claims of the eight configurations I ran, 6.2 per PR, and the judges ranked it first on precision and on writing, but it matched fewer answer-key issues than one Claude Code agent, 37 against 47 of 65. It costs 11 to 14 times as much as /code-review high on the same model, and posts a severity on every finding and an approve or request-changes verdict.


### Why add LLM judges as well as the benchmark’s answer key?


Because the answer key could not separate the leading reviews: three very different setups scored within 0.8 F2 points of each other, and Martian’s key, about 3.7 entries per PR, cannot tell a true claim it lacks from a wrong one. A pairwise judge reads two reviews of the same PR beside the diff, the touched files and the key, and picks the one a maintainer would rather receive. Two judges, GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, each rated 298 matchups with the same prompt; they agreed on precision 76% of the time, on recall 70% and on the overall winner 56%, and the one timed-out max review is absent from the ratings.

## Method and data notes


These notes hold the method, the definitions and the caveats behind every number above, for readers who want them and for AI systems reading this page; the body links to each note by its number.


### 1. What exactly was measured


- **The product.** The local` /code-review` command in Claude Code, a skill bundled with the CLI that runs in your own session on any plan and bills as normal usage or to an API key. With no target it reviews the current branch’s changes, which is the use its documentation describes. The documentation puts a review at[“seconds to a few minutes”](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/ultrareview) , and Anthropic’s engineering post says “/code-review runs a lighter version locally” than the managed service. Anthropic’s docs call the managed service and the local command[“two separate tools”](https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-review-customize) that read different files.
- **What was not measured.** Anthropic’s managed Code Review service (a GitHub App on Team and Enterprise plans, running on Anthropic’s infrastructure, with parallel finders, a verification step and severity tags) and Ultrareview (a cloud review session). Testing the managed service would mean mirroring the benchmark PRs to GitHub with the App installed, a separate project. Nothing in this post is a claim about either of them, or about how Anthropic reviews its own code internally. Martian publishes its own “claude-code” entry on its leaderboard; by its own messages that entry came from the managed service in March 2026, so it appears nowhere here.
- **The version.** Claude Code 2.1.303, the latest release on 2026-10-19 when testing began. It was the latest on all four channels I checked: npm’s` latest` tag, GitHub’s latest release, Anthropic’s download channel and the[CHANGELOG](https://github.com/anthropics/claude-code/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md) (the stable channel was then on 2.1.292). The binary’s sha256 and size matched Anthropic’s release manifest byte for byte, and every line of every session transcript carries` "version": "2.1.303"` . Version 2.1.304 shipped 27 minutes into the 20-PR run; its changelog lists changes to the managed Code Review service and none to the local` /code-review` command, and every run in this post used 2.1.303.
- **Effort levels.** Only` high` and` max` were measured.` low` ,` medium` and` xhigh` were not run.


### 2. How Claude Code ran


-


**Invocation.** The skill alone, typed as a user would type it, with nothing added to the prompt: no PR title or description, no extra prompt, no findings-reporting system prompt, no MCP tool and no permission mode. The benchmark harness’s usual Claude runner appends a findings-reporting prompt; we removed it for these runs. The settings around the skill were ours, and they are part of the measurement: the budget caps and timeouts in the commands below ($5 and 30 minutes for` high` , $30 and 90 minutes for` max` ), the forced subagent model on` max` (` CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL` with` CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1` , note 4), feature-flag fetching off, and default headless permissions. None of these is a shipped default.


```text
# high, one agent
ANTHROPIC_MODEL  =  claude-sonnet-5-5   \
claude   -p   '/code-review high <base>...<head>'   --output-format   json   --max-budget-usd   5
# (and ANTHROPIC_MODEL=claude-opus-5-5 for the Opus 5.5 arm)


# max, every subagent forced to Sonnet 5.5
ANTHROPIC_MODEL  =  claude-opus-5-5   \
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL=claude-sonnet-5-5   \
CLAUDE_CODE_SUBAGENT_MODEL_FORCE=1   \
claude   -p   '/code-review max <base>...<head>'   --output-format   json   --max-budget-usd   30
```


-


**Sandbox.** Each review ran in its own locked-down local Docker container, never against GitHub, with no GitHub token and no GitHub writes. The repository copy held no commits beyond the PR’s base and head (on the one PR we counted, 1,230 commits in the copy and 1,230 in the history up to the head), so the sandbox’s repository history held nothing from the project’s future. That check covers the repository copy and nothing else; it says nothing about what any model saw in training. The API key reached the container through an env file, never on the command line.


-


**Permissions.** Claude Code’s default` -p` permissions, unchanged. Under them WebSearch and WebFetch were refused, and some shell commands needed approval that a headless run cannot give (for example` git -C <path> diff` , while plain` git diff` passes; compound and` python` commands were also refused). The` max` reviews logged 645 refused tool calls in the 14 of the 20 reviews whose output records them, and the two` high` arms 2 and 26 across their 20 reviews each. A refused call costs the agent a turn. Interactive use, where a person approves calls, may behave differently; no permissions-matched run was made.


-


**Feature flags.** Claude Code’s feature-flag fetching was turned off for the scored runs. On browser-use #857 we ran` high` on Opus 5.5 both ways; the review prompt in the transcripts was byte-identical, and both runs found all five defects.


-


**Output.** With` --output-format json` , Claude Code returns the review’s final message. Each finding (file, line, text) went into the scoring pipeline in the same shape as a posted review comment.


### 3. The review recipes we observed


-


**Where they come from.** Each review agent’s prompt in our transcripts opens with a header line naming its recipe. The two we quote are exactly as they appear in 2.1.303 transcripts:


- ` high effort → 8 inline angles → dedup (no verify) → ≤10 findings` , with the instruction to run the eight angles in sequence in its own context rather than spawn subagents;
- ` max effort → 5+5 angles × 8 candidates → 1-vote verify → sweep → ≤15 findings` : about ten finder subagents (on browser-use, five correctness angles, three cleanup angles, an altitude angle and a CLAUDE.md conventions angle, which was skipped because the repository has no CLAUDE.md), then one verifier subagent per candidate, where a single vote that does not refute a finding keeps it, then a sweep for gaps.


The two Claude Code columns of the body’s first figure draw these recipes as the prompt headers describe them, each as its tool intends it; how much of each recipe actually ran depended on the model (note 6).


-

### 9. Failures, and how they were scored


- **Closing notes instead of reviews.** In` -p` mode Claude Code returns only the session’s last message. In a` max` review, verifiers still running in the background report to the main session after the review agent has written its report, and the main session (Opus 5.5) then writes a closing note such as “The last background agents have finished. The report above stands, with no findings to add or remove.” That note is all a script receives. It happened on 5 of the 20 reviews, which delivered 2 of their 63 findings. **Scoring rule:** we scored the review agent’s own last findings report, recovered from the transcripts, and kept the delivered count beside it. We computed no separate as-returned score, so the` max` match counts in the body’s tables are what the reviews found, not what a script would have got back. This rule favours` max` ; scored as delivered, those five PRs would have contributed almost nothing.
- **The timeout.** sentry #67876 ran into our 90-minute limit at 91 minutes and left no report. Its spend is about $23 by the run’s ledger and $24.42 by the last budget line in its transcript; Claude Code recorded no cost for it. **Scoring rule:** zero findings on the answer key, and in the Elo ratings the PR drops out of that configuration’s pairs (the judge cannot compare a review that does not exist), so` max` is rated on 19 PRs and the Elo carries no penalty for the missing review.
- **Rate limits.** Our API key’s limits are 50 requests a minute for Opus 5.5, 1,000 for Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, and 500,000 input and 80,000 output tokens a minute per model. Anthropic’s[published rate limits](https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/api/rate-limits) give the standard Start tier 1,000 requests, 2,000,000 input tokens and 400,000 output tokens a minute for these models, and say new organizations may start in an Evaluation tier below the standard limits. On the one-PR trial run, one` max` review with Sonnet 5.5 agents averaged about 20,000 output tokens a minute and peaked near 65,000. We started at 3 reviews at a time, went to 5, then 4, and back to 3 after reviews began failing. 25 of the 339 agents ended on 429 errors that their retries did not recover: 23 of them in 11 finished reviews that still reported success, and 2 in the review that timed out. One review (grafana #90045, $12.27) died on 429s before writing its report and was re-run; in the scored reviews every agent that died on a 429 was a finder or verifier, never the review agent itself. After the drop back to 3 at a time no more reviews died on 429s. These failures come from our key’s limits and our concurrency, not from a defect in Claude Code, but they show that a successful exit status does not mean every agent ran.
- **Our own operator errors.** Two reviews (cal.com #10600, about $5 spent, and sentry-greptile #3, about $2.40) were killed when a queue runner was paused and the tool that launched it killed its process group; both were re-run from scratch. Rebuilding the harness image briefly made the queue lose track of running reviews, so 8 ran at once for about a minute; the 4 surplus reviews (33 seconds old) were killed and re-queued. The partial attempts were kept on disk for the record and never scored.
- **Quickchat Review’s failures.** On Sonnet 5.5, the main session ran none of its planned passes and no validator on 2 of the 20 PRs (“I skipped the lens passes and the validator and reviewed the diff myself”; one of those went out as an approval) and launched fewer passes than planned on 3 more; it also dropped some candidates “to save effort” before the validator. **Scoring rule:** scored as delivered, the same as Claude Code’s timeout. On Opus 5.5 every planned pass and the validator launched on every PR, and 6 throttled calls were retried. All 20 reviews finished in both arms. This is why the body calls the validator “meant to” keep old bugs out: on these builds the planned passes and the validator are asked for by the prompt and not enforced by the harness, so what was observed (every stage on Opus 5.5, stages skipped on 2 of 20 PRs on Sonnet 5.5) sits beside what is intended. The one finding per root cause, the severity and the verdict were observed on every review.
- **Completion.** Claude Code` high` finished 40 of 40 reviews on the 20 PRs (and 70 of 70 Martian reviews in all);` max` finished 19 of 20, and 14 of those 19 returned their report to the caller.


### 10. The pairwise judge


-


**Why.** The answer key separated` max` (F2 30.0) from the leaders but not the leaders from each other. On the 20 PRs, three very different setups scored within 0.8 points of each other on F2: Quickchat Review on Sonnet 5.5 at 43.9, Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.5 at 43.2 and Claude Code` high` on Sonnet 5.5 at 43.1, a spread these data cannot separate (note 7). The key holds about 3.7 entries per PR (74 on these 20), while the reviews we ran made about 8 to 26 claims per PR, and the key cannot tell a true claim it lacks from a wrong one; both count against precision. A one-line review that matches one key entry and a thorough review that finds three real bugs the key lacks can score alike. The pairwise judge was added after those scores were in, to read whole reviews against the code: it reads two reviews of the same PR side by side and picks a winner, and a rating fitted over many such judgments separates configurations the answer key compresses together.


-


**One judgment is one model call.** No tools, no agent loop, structured JSON output, and each answer accepted only as one plain final message (checked on every call: a cut-off, tool call or refusal counts as an error and is retried, at most 3 attempts).


-


**What the prompt holds, in order.** The PR’s title and description; its diff; every file it touches as it is at the head commit, line-numbered; Martian’s answer-key comments; then Review A and Review B (findings and summary). Lockfiles, checksum files, minified bundles and source maps are left out and replaced by one line with their changed-line counts. The prompt ceiling is 400,000 tokens; past it, the largest files fall back to their diff with 60 lines of context (on these 20 PRs no prompt reached the ceiling). The judge sees the touched files only, not the callers, dependencies or tests a reviewer could open, so it cannot check every claim a review makes; it has no “insufficient context” verdict.


-


**Identity labels removed.** Both reviews are rewritten into one neutral shape: path, lines, text and, where the review stated one, a severity. Quickchat Review’s pass labels, footers and signature are stripped and its tags become a stated severity; Claude Code’s JSON dump of its own findings is removed from its summary. A and B order is random, drawn once per pair, and no pair was judged in both orders. The judge is told not to guess which tool wrote which review, but a stated severity, the number of findings and the writing style remain, so tool identity may stay inferable.


-


**The answer key is a reference, not truth.** The judge may decide that a finding outside the key is a real defect, or that a key comment is wrong, but only by pointing at code in the prompt (file, line, what it does); without that evidence it defers to the key. An unmatched finding is a false positive only when the code shows it is wrong, the failure cannot happen, or it is noise a maintainer would not want. No sample of these decisions was checked by a human.


-


**The verdict.** Four categories, each with reasoning first and then a winner (A, B or tie):


- **recall:** which review catches more of the real defects that matter, key comments plus real defects the key lacks, weighted by severity;
- **precision:** which spends less of the author’s attention on findings that are wrong, unreachable or not worth raising;
- **finding quality:** for the real findings, correct severity, precise location, a concrete failure scenario, the root cause and an actionable fix;
- **writing:** which a developer can read and act on faster.


Then the overall question: “which review a maintainer of this repository would rather have received on this pull request. Catching the serious defects and not wasting the author’s time matter most; finding quality next; writing can decide a close call.” The judge is told that more findings, longer text and confident tone earn nothing on their own, and that several comments about one root cause count as one finding.


-


**The two judges.** GPT-6.1 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5, both at xhigh reasoning effort, with an identical prompt. Every judgment records the sha256 of the exact prompt it saw. When a PR’s prompt changed (28 GPT judgments were made before we stopped packing lockfiles whole), those judgments were set aside and the pair was judged again by both judges, so both judges’ ratings rest on the same prompts.


### 11. How the Elo ratings were calculated


-


**What is rated.** A configuration’s review of a PR enters the ratings only if it exists, and the five` max` reports recovered from transcripts enter as recovered. The ratings are therefore conditional on an available report, with transcript recovery; the timed-out` max` review is absent, so` max` is rated on 19 PRs and the other configurations on 20. The body’s “over the reviews that exist” and every Elo it quotes mean exactly this.


-


**The fit.** Each judgment is one game between two configurations on one PR: 1 for a win, 0.5 for a tie, 0 for a loss. Ratings are a regularized maximum-likelihood fit of the[Bradley-Terry model](https://doi.org/10.2307/2334029) (Bradley and Terry, 1952), computed with[Hunter’s MM iteration](https://doi.org/10.1214/aos/1079120141) (Hunter, 2004), with half a virtual tie between every pair as the regularizer so that a configuration that wins every game still gets a finite rating. Ratings are shown on the Elo scale, 1500 + 400 × log10(strength relative to the geometric mean).[Chatbot Arena](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04132) likewise ranks models by Bradley-Terry coefficients fitted to pairwise preferences. Under the fitted model a 100-point gap is an expected score of about 64% for the higher one and 148 points about 70%; those are the model’s expected scores within this evaluation, not measured probabilities that a maintainer prefers a review. The body’s “about a 70% expected win rate” for the +148 gap is this figure. The fitting code ships with the raw results (note 16).


-


**The intervals.** 95% intervals from 1,000 bootstrap samples over PRs, not over games: judgments on one PR share its difficulty, so the PR is the unit resampled. The ratings’ intervals and every gap’s interval come from the same bootstrap draw. They are pointwise and not adjusted for the number of comparisons made. Because later rounds were allocated after inspecting the earlier ratings (below), they are exploratory and conditional on the matchups that were sampled. A gap is called clear when its interval excludes zero.


-


**Sampling.** Round 0 judged every pair of the 8 configurations (28 pairs) on the same 5 PRs, 140 judgments per judge. An adaptive round then gave 3 fresh PRs to each of 6 pairs of neighbouring configurations whose gap interval still crossed zero (18 judgments). A final targeted round judged every pair among the top five combined configurations (` max` , Quickchat Review on Opus 5.5, on GPT-6.1 Sol and on Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.5) on every PR not yet judged (140 judgments), so those five were compared pairwise on every available PR. That made 298 judgments per judge over all 20 PRs, under a cap of 300. The three lowest configurations (Quickchat Review on DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and on GLM-5.3 Flash, and Claude Code` high` on Sonnet 5.5) were not in the final round, so their ratings rest mostly on round 0 and have wider intervals; that includes Claude Code` high` on Sonnet 5.5, which appears in the body’s main table.


-


**Combining the judges.** Each judge is fitted on its own, and the combined table counts every PR-pair both judges answered once per judge, at equal weight (596 games). Equal weight is a chosen aggregation rule, not a correction for either judge’s bias. Win-tie-loss counts quoted for the combined table (such as` max` ’s 162-22-10 on recall, over the 194 recall verdicts on its pairs) are over those 596 games.

### 12. Judge agreement and self-preference


- **Agreement over the 298 matchups both judges answered.** Same overall winner 56%, opposite 44% (no overall ties). Recall 70% same and 7% opposite; precision 76% and 7%; finding quality 50% and 26%; writing 74% and 20%. The rest are matchups where one judge called a tie. These are raw agreement rates, affected by how often each verdict occurs; agreement between two LLM judges says they read the reviews alike, not that either read them correctly, and no human calibration of the verdicts was made.
- **Each judge’s top configuration ran on its own family.** The GPT judge’s table is led by Quickchat Review on GPT-6.1 Sol (1738, 73 wins and 21 losses); the Opus judge’s by Claude Code` max` (1883, 88 wins and 9 losses), a Claude-written review that also carries the most findings. The two judges agree almost exactly on Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.5 (1514 and 1512). The pattern fits a family preference; it also fits two judges valuing coverage and brevity differently, and these data cannot separate the two explanations. The body’s “GPT favoured lean reviews and Opus thorough ones” is the observed pattern, not a settled cause.
- **How they weigh the overall question.** In 12 matchups we read before the full run, GPT resolved the overall verdict toward precision (“A’s precision problems are decisive”) and Opus toward recall (“A maintainer would get more of the expected defects from A, with only modest noise”). In a handful of spot checks, a third judge (DeepSeek V4.1 Flash, an open model) sided with Opus more often than with GPT.
- **What follows.** The per-category results are where the judges mostly agree on which review has more recall, more precision and better writing, so they depend less on which judge one trusts. The overall winner is a weighting of recall against noise, and that is a value judgment. Combining two judges from different providers at equal weight is a chosen rule that limits how far either judge’s preference can carry the table; it does not show that the preference is gone.

### 15. Limitations


- 20 PRs from one benchmark, chosen non-randomly, plus Claude Code` high` on Opus 5.5 and four configurations of Quickchat Review on all 50. One run per configuration, so run-to-run variance is unknown, and the “about two issues” of noise is a prior from earlier repeated scoring, not a measurement made here.
- Two LLM judges, both from families with a configuration in the pool, and each putting a configuration from its own family first. The answer-key judge is a third LLM. No judgment was checked by a human.
- The overall Elo question left the weight of recall against noise to the judges, and they weighed it differently. The Elo ratings are conditional on an available report, with transcript recovery, so the timed-out` max` review costs it nothing there; the later judging rounds were allocated after inspecting earlier ratings, so the intervals are exploratory.
- The` max` arm forced Sonnet 5.5 subagents and ran under a $30 cap whose budget line the agents could see and acted on (note 3); the all-Opus configuration was measured on one PR only, where our 30-minute limit stopped it. An uncapped all-Opus` max` on the 20 PRs was not run.
- Costs are as each tool records or computes them: Claude Code’s are its own list-price estimates, except the $40.64, which is our recount; Quickchat Review’s are computed at list prices from its token usage; the Opus 5.5 main session added 0.44% of the` max` arm’s cost (note 8).
- Our API key’s rate limits are below Anthropic’s standard tier, which caused the 429 failures and limited concurrency; on a higher tier` max` reviews would likely fail less and finish sooner. Every time in this post is wall-clock under those limits and our concurrency, and no run was made at matched concurrency.
- Claude Code ran with default` -p` permissions in a sandbox where its web tools and some shell commands were refused, under our sandbox configuration (feature-flag fetching off, forced subagent models on` max` , budget caps of $5 and $30, timeouts of 30 and 90 minutes); interactive use, where a person approves tool calls, may behave differently.
- The same-model rows compare complete configurations that share a primary model (note 4): Quickchat Review read the PR title, description and dependency sources, ran six passes on GPT-6 Luna and used its own permissions; Claude Code did none of that.
- The recommendation to start with` high` on Opus 5.5 rests on 51 of 66 serious issues matched on all 50 PRs, which also means 15 missed; whether that is enough for a given repository or risk is not something this benchmark can say.
- The browser-use answer key (note 6) is our own and was built and checked by AI agents with no human check, and the scoring of that PR had no human check either.
- A one-shot benchmark sees only a first review. Neither tool’s follow-up rounds, replies to the author or repository-specific setup were exercised.
